---
title: "Data states, codebooks and provenance"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

A file called `final_clean_v7` leaves quite a few questions unanswered. You need to know where it came from, what changed in version seven and why rows are missing.

You can make those answers easy to find. Keep the original data, record each transformation and write down what the fields mean. The history is called *provenance*; the guide to the fields is a *data dictionary* or *codebook*. Both help you return to an analysis months later without having to reconstruct every decision from memory.

## Give each version a clear purpose {#make-every-data-state-and-transformation-explainable}

“Clean” can mean several things. Perhaps you corrected dates, removed duplicates or created new variables. Name those steps and keep their rules, so someone else can follow the changes from the original data to a result.

Keep the original source protected from overwrite. Later versions should tell you what changed, why, when, who made the change and which records were excluded.

## Define the states for this project

A practical sequence is:

| State | Meaning | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Incoming | received but not yet verified, quarantined or registered | do not analyse |
| Raw authoritative | closest retained representation of the approved source or capture | preserve and protect from overwrite |
| Interim or working | parsing, transcription, coding or quality work in progress | disposable only if reproducible and authorised |
| Derived | new variables, features, categories, segments or aggregations | transformation and inputs must be recorded |
| Analysis-ready | fixed input prepared for a named analysis under defined rules | version, schema and exclusions frozen for that analysis |
| Release | reviewed material approved for a particular audience and use | separate privacy, licence and disclosure check |

These names may not fit every project. A historian may preserve photographed archival pages, transcription, annotations and interpretive corpus. A qualitative project may separate original audio, verified transcript, coded corpus and publication extracts. An imaging study may preserve instrument-native files, calibrated images, segmented objects and analysis tables.

## Keep the original source {#protect-the-earliest-authoritative-state}

Raw does not mean perfect, neutral or free from prior processing. Device firmware, platform exports, transcription services, laboratory systems and data custodians may already have transformed the source.

On receipt or capture, retain:

- source, custodian and authority;
- date/time and transfer route;
- original filename and format;
- file manifest, checksum or equivalent identity;
- instrument, software, firmware or export settings;
- schema and record count where relevant;
- known missingness, truncation or corruption;
- consent, licence or use constraints; and
- the person who verified receipt.

If correction of the source record is necessary, preserve the original and create a documented corrected version. Do not silently edit values in place.

## Record every change to the data

Prefer scripts, queries or structured workflows that can be rerun. Where manual judgement is necessary, preserve a decision log or annotation record containing:

- input record and location;
- original value or interpretation;
- changed value, code or classification;
- rule or rationale;
- person and date;
- reviewer where required;
- uncertainty or disagreement; and
- effect on downstream states.

Spreadsheet editing can be appropriate, but hidden cell changes, sorting errors and overwritten formulas are difficult to audit. Retain imports, use validation, protect identifier columns, export change logs where possible and compare outputs to expectations.

## Keep the data trail

For every published number, quotation, image or model, aim to trace:

`output → analysis or interpretation → analysis-ready input → derivation/selection → raw authoritative source → authority and context`

Forward provenance answers what a source record influenced. Backward provenance answers where a result came from. Both matter for correction.

Record:

- stable dataset or corpus IDs;
- versions or release tags;
- checksums or manifests for important files;
- code commit, script or workflow version;
- configuration and parameters;
- inclusion, exclusion and missing-data decisions;
- software/environment information;
- person or automated process responsible; and
- date and outcome of checks.

ARDC includes documentation, metadata, provenance and versioning within good data practice [@ardc-good-data]. Apply these principles in a way proportionate to the research and consistent with data governance.

## Explain the fields in a data dictionary {#use-a-data-dictionary-as-a-contract}

For tabular or structured data, each variable should specify:

- dataset and variable name;
- plain-language definition;
- construct or source field;
- unit, type and allowed values;
- coding and missing-value rules;
- collection or derivation method;
- time reference and level of observation;
- applicable population or records;
- sensitivity and release status;
- validation checks;
- known limitations; and
- owner and version.

For qualitative or unstructured material, a codebook may instead record code name, definition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, examples, boundaries, relationships, decision history and unresolved disagreements.

A dictionary documents meaning. It does not establish that a measure is valid.

## Example: the changing status variable

Five yearly extracts contain a column called `STATUS`, with values `A`, `I`, `W`, `T`, blank and `0`. It looks easy to turn `A` into “active”, `W` into “withdrawn” and everything else into missing data.

The custodian explains that `I` changed from “inactive” to “interrupted” in 2024. In different legacy systems, `T` covers transfer or completion. Zero is an export default, and a blank sometimes means there is no current enrolment row.

Keep each original extract and its period-specific definitions. Create separate fields for the source status and the harmonised status, retaining “unknown” where you cannot establish the meaning. Check a sample against the recorded histories. If the years cannot be compared reliably, restrict the analysis period or narrow the claim.

## Record exclusions as data decisions

For every exclusion rule, document:

- why it exists;
- when it was decided;
- whether it was prespecified or observed after inspection;
- records affected;
- whether the exclusion differs across analyses;
- effect on target population or corpus;
- sensitivity or alternative analysis; and
- approval or review where required.

Never delete excluded records from the only dataset. Preserve a status or flow record so counts can be reconciled.

## Validate each state transition

Automate checks where practical:

- input file identity and schema;
- unique and non-missing identifiers;
- row, case, file or segment counts;
- allowable values and units;
- date ranges and ordering;
- impossible combinations;
- duplicate and linkage behaviour;
- transformations on known test cases;
- reconciliation of exclusions;
- unexpected disclosure fields; and
- output schema and checksum.

A pipeline that completes without an error may still produce the wrong data. Include tests tied to scientific and operational expectations.

## Handle new source versions deliberately

When a collaborator sends `dataset_final.xlsx` again:

1. retain both files without overwriting;
2. register receipt, source and checksum;
3. compare schema, records and values;
4. ask what changed and why;
5. determine which version is authoritative for which period or purpose;
6. rerun affected transformations in a new state/version;
7. compare downstream results; and
8. record the decision and disclosure consequence.

Do not assume the latest attachment supersedes the prior research record.

## Follow one result back to its source

Choose a number, quotation or image from your draft. Can you find its input, the transformation or selection rule, and the original source? Check the dictionary along the way. Blank, zero, `NA`, “unknown” and “not applicable” may mean different things.

Before analysis, fix the input version for that analysis and reconcile the exclusions. Before release, check privacy and permitted use separately. If a field is unclear, take the source definition, transformation script, difficult record and test result to the custodian or supervisor. The [data dictionary](../../templates/data-dictionary.qmd) gives you somewhere to record the answer.
